source_text: Ἵνα δὲ μὴ παρέλθωμεν τὰ ἐν τοῖς μεταξὺ λελεγμένα τῷ Κέλσῳ, φέρ᾿ ἐκθώμεθα καὶ ταῦτα. χρήσαιτο δ᾿ ἄν τις καὶ Ἡροδότῳ πρὸς τόδε μάρτυρι, λέγοντι ὧδε· „οἱ γὰρ δὴ ἐκ Μαρέης τε πόλιος καὶ Ἄπιος οἰκέοντες Αἰγύπτου τὰ πρόσουρα Λιβύῃ. αὐτοί τε δοκέοντες εἶναι Λίβυες καὶ οὐκ Αἰγύπτιοι καὶ ἀχθόμενοι τῇ περὶ τὰ ἱερὰ θρησκείῃ, βουλόμενοι θηλέων βοῶν μὴ ἔργεσθαι, ἔπεμψαν ἐς Ἄμμωνα φάμενοι οὐδὲν σφίσι τε καὶ Αἰγυπτίοισι κοινὸν εἶναι· οἰκέειν γὰρ ἔξω τοῦ Δέλτα καὶ οὐχ ὁμολογέειν αὐτοῖσι, βούλεσθαί τε πάντων σφίσιν ἐξεῖναι γεύεσθαι. ὁ δὲ θεὸς οὐκ ἔα σφέας ποιέειν ταῦτα, φὰς Αἴγυπτον εἶναι ταύτην, τὴν ὁ Νεῖλος ἐπιὼν ἄρδει. καὶ Αἰγυπτίους εἶναι τούτους, οἳ ἔνερθεν Ἐλεφαντίνης πόλιος οἰκέοντες ἀπὸ τοῦ ποταμοῦ τούτου πίνουσιν.“ Ἡροδότῳ μὲν τάδε ἱστόρηται. ὁ δ᾿ Ἄμμων οὐδέν τι κακίων διαπρεσβεῦσαι τὰ δαιμόνια ἢ οἱ Ἰουδαίων ἄγγελοι· ὥστε οὐδὲν ἄδικον ἑκάστους τὰ σφέτερα νόμιμα θρησκεύειν. ἀμέλει πλεῖστον αὐτῶν εὑρήσομεν κατα ἔθνη τὸ διαφέρον, καὶ ὅμως ἕκαστοι αὐτοὶ μάλιστα ευ νομίζειν δοκοῦσιν· Αἰθιόπων μὲν οἱ Μερόην οἰκοῦντες „Δία καὶ Διόνυσον μόνους“ σέβοντες, Ἀράβιοι δὲ τὴν Οὐρανίαν καὶ Διόνυσον τούτους μόνους. Αἰγύπτιοι δὲ πάντες μὲν Ὄσιρίν τε καὶ Ἶσιν, Σαῗται δὲ Ἀθηνᾶν, Ναυκρατῖται δὲ, οὐ πάλαι ἀρξάμενοι, ὠνόμασαν Σάραπιν, καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ κατὰ νομοὺς ὡς ἕκαστοι. καὶ οἱ μὲν ὀΐων ἀπέχονται, σέβοντες ὡς ἱεροὺς, οἱ δὲ αἰγῶν, οἱ δὲ κροκοδείλων. οἱ δὲ βοῶν θηλειῶν, συῶν δὲ ἀπέχονται βδελυττόμενοι. Σκύθαις γε μὴν καὶ ἀνθρώπους δαίνυσθαι καλόν· Ἰνδῶν δέ εἰσιν οἳ καὶ τοὺς πατέρας ἐσθίοντες ὅσια δρᾶν νομίζουσι. καὶ που φησὶν ὁ αὐτὸς Ἡρόδοτος· χρήσομαι δὲ αὖθις αὐταῖς ἐκείνου λέξεσι πίστεως εἵνεκα· ἱστορεῖ δὲ ὧδε· „εἰ γάρ τις προθείη πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποισιν ἐκλέξασθαι κελεύων νόμους τοὺς καλλίστους ἐκ (τῶν) πάντων νόμων, διασκεψάμενοι ἂν ἑλοίατο (ἕκαστοι τοὺς ἑωυτῶν· οὕτω νομίζουσι) πολλόν τι καλλίστους (τοὺς) ἑωυτῶν νόμους ἕκαστοι εἶναι. οὔκων εἰκός ἐστιν ἄλλον γε ἢ μαινόμενον ἄνδρα (γέλωτα) τὰ τοιαῦτα τίθεσθαι. ὡς δ᾿ οὕτως νενομίκασι τὰ περὶ τοὺς νόμους οἱ πάντες ἄνθρωποι, πολλοῖσι καὶ ἄλλοισι τεκμηρίοισι πάρεστι σταθμώσασθαι, ἐν δὲ δὴ καὶ (τῷδε) . Δαρεῖος ἐπὶ τῆς ἑωυτοῦ ἀρχῆς καλέσας Ἑλλήνων τοὺς παρεόντας εἴρετο ἐπὶ κόσῳ ἂν χρήματι βουλοίατο τοὺς πατέρας ἀποθνῄσκοντας κατασιτέεσθαι· οἱ δὲ ἔφασαν ἐπ᾿ οὐδενὶ ἕρδειν ἂν τοῦτο. Δαρεῖος δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα καλέσας Ἰνδῶν τοὺς καλεομένους Καλατίας, οἳ τοὺς γονέας κατεσθίουσιν, εἴρετο, παρεόντων τῶν Ἑλλήνων καὶ δι᾿ ἑρμηνέος μανθανόντων τὰ λεγόμενα, ἐπὶ τίνι χρήματι δεξαίατ᾿ ἂν τελευτέοντας τοὺς πατέρας κατακαίειν πυρί· οἱ δὲ ἀμβώσαντες μέγα εὐφημέειν μιν ἐκέλευον. οὕτω μὲν νῦν ταῦτα νενόμισται, καὶ ὀρθῶς μοι δοκέει Πίνδαρος ποιῆσαι, νόμον πάντων βασιλέα φήσας εἶναι.“
thought_title: Celsus calls Herodotus to witness for ancestral custom
pass_a_gloss: So that we may not pass over (παρέλθωμεν) what was said by Celsus in between (ἐν τοῖς μεταξύ), come, let us set out (ἐκθώμεθα) these too. [Celsus:] One might use (χρήσαιτο) Herodotus too as witness (μάρτυρι) for this, saying thus: [Hdt. 2.18, Ionic:] those from the city (πόλις) of Marea and Apis, inhabiting the parts of Egypt bordering (πρόσουρα) Libya, themselves seeming/thinking to be Libyans and not Egyptians, and being vexed (ἀχθόμενοι) at the ritual (θρησκείη) concerning sacred things (ἱερά), wishing not to be barred (ἔργεσθαι) from female cattle (θήλεαι βόες), sent to Ammon saying that there is nothing common (κοινόν) to them and Egyptians; for they live outside the Delta and do not agree (ὁμολογέειν) with them, and wish to be permitted to taste (γεύεσθαι) of all things. But the god (θεός) did not allow them to do this, saying that this is Egypt which the Nile coming upon (ἐπιών) waters (ἄρδει), and those are Egyptians who, living below (ἔνερθεν) the city of Elephantine, drink from this river. These things are related (ἱστόρηται) by Herodotus. But Ammon [is] in no way worse (κακίων) at conveying as envoy (διαπρεσβεῦσαι) the divine things (τὰ δαιμόνια) than the angels (ἄγγελοι) of the Jews; so that [it is] nothing unjust (ἄδικον) for each to practise religiously (θρησκεύειν) their own customs (νόμιμα). Certainly (ἀμέλει) we shall find the difference (τὸ διαφέρον) of them greatest by nations (κατὰ ἔθνη), and yet each themselves seem most of all to hold customs well (εὖ νομίζειν): of Ethiopians those inhabiting Meroe revering (σέβοντες) Zeus and Dionysus alone (μόνους), Arabians Urania and Dionysus, these alone; Egyptians all Osiris and Isis, Saites Athena, Naucratites, having begun not long ago (οὐ πάλαι), named (ὠνόμασαν) Serapis, and the rest according to nomes (νομοί) as each. And some abstain (ἀπέχονται) from sheep (ὄϊς), revering them as sacred (ἱερούς), others from goats, others from crocodiles, others from female cattle, and they abstain from pigs loathing (βδελυττόμενοι) them. To Scythians it is fine (καλόν) even to feast on (δαίνυσθαι) men; of Indians there are those who, eating even their fathers, think they do holy things (ὅσια δρᾶν). And somewhere the same Herodotus says, and I will use again his very words (λέξεσι) for the sake of credibility (πίστεως εἵνεκα); he relates thus: [Hdt. 3.38:] if one should set before (προθείη) all men, bidding (κελεύων) them choose (ἐκλέξασθαι) the finest customs (νόμους καλλίστους) out of all customs, having examined (διασκεψάμενοι) they would choose (ἑλοίατο) — each their own; so (οὕτω) they hold (νομίζουσι) their own customs to be by far (πολλόν τι) the finest. So it is not likely (εἰκός) that anyone other than a madman (μαινόμενον) would make such things a laughing-stock (γέλωτα τίθεσθαι). That all men have so held about customs one may judge (σταθμώσασθαι) by many other proofs (τεκμήρια), and among them by this: Darius in his reign (ἀρχή), calling the Greeks present, asked for how much money (κόσῳ = πόσῳ χρήματι) they would be willing to eat up (κατασιτέεσθαι) their fathers when dying; they said for nothing (ἐπ᾿ οὐδενί) would they do (ἕρδειν) this. Darius after this, calling of the Indians those called Callatiae, who eat (κατεσθίουσιν) their parents (γονέας), asked, the Greeks being present and learning what was said through an interpreter (ἑρμηνεύς), for what money they would accept (δεξαίατο) to burn up (κατακαίειν) with fire their fathers when they died; they, crying out (ἀμβώσαντες) loudly, bade him keep holy silence / speak no ill-omened word (εὐφημέειν). So now these things are customary (νενόμισται), and rightly, it seems to me, Pindar composed (ποιῆσαι), declaring custom (νόμος) king (βασιλεύς) of all.

pass_b_english: So that we do not pass over what Celsus said in the passage between, let us set this out as well. “One might also call on Herodotus as a witness to this, who says as follows: ‘The people of the city of Marea and of Apis, who live in the parts of Egypt bordering on Libya, thought themselves Libyans and not Egyptians, and chafed at the observance of the sacred rites, since they did not wish to be barred from cows. So they sent to Ammon, saying that they had nothing in common with the Egyptians, for they lived outside the Delta and did not agree with them, and that they wished to be allowed to taste of everything. But the god would not let them do this. He said that Egypt was the land which the Nile overflows and waters, and that those were Egyptians who live below the city of Elephantine and drink from this river’ (Herodotus, Histories 2.18). That is Herodotus’s account. But Ammon is no worse an envoy of divine things than the angels of the Jews, so that there is nothing wrong in each people practising its own customs.

“Indeed we shall find the greatest difference among them from nation to nation, and yet each people seems to think its own customs the best of all. Of the Ethiopians, those who live at Meroe worship ‘Zeus and Dionysus alone’ (Herodotus, Histories 2.29); the Arabians worship Urania and Dionysus, these alone (Herodotus, Histories 3.8). All the Egyptians worship Osiris and Isis; the people of Sais worship Athena; the people of Naucratis, who began not long ago, have named Serapis; and the rest each in their own way, nome by nome. Some abstain from sheep, revering them as sacred, others from goats, others from crocodiles, others from cows, and they abstain from pigs because they loathe them. Among the Scythians it is a fine thing even to feast on men, and there are Indians who think they do a holy thing by eating even their fathers.

“And somewhere the same Herodotus says (I will again use his very words, so as to be believed), and his account runs thus: ‘If one were to set before all men the task of choosing the finest customs out of all customs, each, after looking them over, would choose their own, so firmly does each people believe its own customs to be by far the finest. It is not likely, then, that anyone but a madman would make a mockery of such things. That all men hold this view about customs may be judged from many other proofs, and among them from this one. Darius, during his reign, called the Greeks who were present and asked them for what sum they would be willing to eat their fathers when they died. They said that they would not do it for any sum. After this Darius called the Indians known as Callatiae, who eat their parents, and asked them, while the Greeks were present and learned through an interpreter what was said, for what sum they would agree to burn their fathers with fire when they died. They cried out loudly and told him to speak no words of ill omen. So these things are fixed by custom, and Pindar, I think, put it rightly in his verse when he said that custom is king of all’ (Herodotus, Histories 3.38; Pindar, fragment 169).”
notes: The whole chapter after Origen's first sentence is Celsus's text, with two long verbatim quotations of Herodotus nested inside it (single quotation marks). Celsus himself says he quotes Herodotus's very words (Herodotus, Histories 2.18 and 3.38); the intervening catalogue of cults draws on Herodotus 2.29 (Meroe: Zeus and Dionysus), 3.8 (Arabians: Dionysus and Urania), and Egyptian material in book 2, but the Serapis line is Celsus's own (Herodotus does not mention Serapis). Only the certain Herodotus loci are cited inline. Pindar's line 'custom is king of all' is Pindar, fragment 169 (Snell-Maehler 169a), quoted by Herodotus. Koetschau's text of Herodotus 3.38 carries editorial supplements in parentheses from the Herodotus manuscripts: (τῶν), (ἕκαστοι τοὺς ἑωυτῶν· οὕτω νομίζουσι), (τοὺς), (γέλωτα), (τῷδε); the translation follows the supplemented text, since without them the sentence does not construe. κόσῳ is Ionic for πόσῳ. θηλέων βοῶν μὴ ἔργεσθαι: 'not to be barred from cows', i.e. from eating them; the Egyptians did not eat cows (sacred to Isis). τὰ δαιμόνια in Celsus's mouth is neutral ('divine things'), rendered 'divine things', not 'demons'. εὐφημέειν literally 'to keep holy silence / speak well-omened words', rendered 'speak no words of ill omen'. ὠνόμασαν Σάραπιν rendered literally 'have named Serapis' (i.e. adopted him as their god). Typos in the staged Greek (κατα, ευ, ουν, καταλι πόντας in the next chapter) are spacing/accent losses from the TEI and do not affect sense. No Scripture in this chapter.
